catalog_quote: Stress is normally assigned to the penultimate syllable of a word or compound. This penultimate position shifts with affixation, so that, for instances, we have /mena/ /mena-do/ /mena-na-o/ dog dog-IND dog-PL-IND ... Exceptions to this are found if a) the root ends in a nasal, or b) all the vowels in the word are the same (the presence of one of the heavy consonants in a word might also affect stress, as discussed in section 2.3). In the event that the root ends in a nasal, and there are two non-contiguous vowels, we find that stress does not shift with the addition of suffixes. ... A word with a final nasal, but with all contiguous vowels, such as /nuan/ 'coconut' ... behaves normally, with penultimate stress ... Should all the vowels of a word be identical, then stress is ultimate, not penultimate: [ ] 'fruit', [ ] 'round'. In compounds, the primary stress stays with the first compone…

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation, the heavy-consonant passage and the domain quote are all verbatim in the Donohue PDF we hold/txt at the stated sections and annotated-version pages (2 intro p. 5; 2.2 pp. 7-8; 2.3 pp. 8-9; 2.4 p. 9). (2) Deciding source: a 1999 Lincom grammar sketch (iv+64 pp) by the only linguist to have worked on the language, read in the author's own full annotated text; impressionistic, hedged by the author, but it is the entire descriptive literature on Warembori phonology. Glottolog 5.1's other 'descriptive' refs are a DM reanalysis of verb inflection (Hein et al. 2008), a mis-attached 1988 book review, and an 1885 wordlist; Wikipedia's phonology section rests on Donohue 1999 and Foley's 2018 survey chapter (p. 502), which restates Donohue; Crossref has no Warembori works.
